name: Kurdish
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: stress the final syllable of a PW. ... we propose that a distinction should be made between word-level and phrase-level stress in NK ... The phrase stress falls on the first PW in the PP.
sweep_summary: Northern Kurdish (nort2641, catalog fixed-strict final). this search of works with stress in the title produced a single title, Shokri 2002 'Syllable structure and stress in Bahdinani Kurdish' (STUF 55(1): 80-97, Haig & Matras Kurdish special issue): squarely about word stress in this language (Bahdinani = Duhok Kurmanji), but closed on every OA index (Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar) and De Gruyter's site is behind an AWS-WAF challenge; Hasan 2016 p.370 cites it as one of the sources for final stress irrespective of syllable weight, so it is expected to confirm the classification; acquisition priority medium (a peer-reviewed 17-page treatment of the same variety our best held source describes, useful as an independent citable statement, but the catalog is already well-sourced). Held open sources re-read in this search of works with stress in the title: Hasan 2016 (ESJ, open) p.370 and p.379 rule 30 'stress the final syllable of a PW' — the catalog's own deciding quote, whose cite field is empty and whose page locators should be 379/393; Bedir Khan & Lescot 1970 §77-78 (pp.49-50) 'il porte généralement sur la dernière syllabe.. dans certains cas.. sur l'avant-dernière', any vowel long or short — confirms final default, refines with a small penult class (-ik, concrete -î). no reclassification indicated; action: fill catalog_cite with Hasan 2016: 379, 393 and add B&L 1970 §§77-81 as corroboration.

new_statements.quote: p.370: 'Kurdish is known to have a simple stress rule that places stress on the word final syllable irrespective of its length or syllable weight (Bedir Khan and Lescot, 1970; Fattah, 1980; Qadir, 1983; Ahmed, 1986; Shokri, 2002).' p.379: 'Based on previous descriptions of Kurdish word stress which suggest that stress is placed on the word final syllable (Fattah, 1980; Qadir, 1983; Ahmed, 1986) ... we will identify the PW as the domain of stress: 30- NK word stress-assignment rule: stress the final syllable of a PW. ... In these examples, stress is assigned to the PW ultimate syllable which might be a simple word as in (a), a sequence of a stem+suffix as in (b & c), a sequence of prefix+stem as in (d), a compound as in (e) and a sequence of proclitic+lexical word as in (f).'
new_statements.citation: Hasan, Aveen Mohammed. 2016. The phonological word and stress shift in Northern Kurmanji Kurdish. European Scientific Journal 12(26): 370-398. doi:10.19044/esj.2016.v12n26p370 (open access)

new_statements.reading: Fixed final stress, quantity-insensitive, domain = phonological word (stem plus affixes, compounds, proclitic+host); examples 'xoş, xoş'tir, xoşti'rîn, di'gut, guneh'bar, ji 'mal. Exceptions (adverbs/conjunctions with heavy penult, stressed negative/mood prefixes) are handled as stress shift or as separate PWs with phrase stress on the first PW (p.393). This is the very source of the catalog's deciding quotation, whose 'catalog_cite' field is empty: it should read Hasan 2016: 379 (rule 30) and 393 (word- vs phrase-level stress), not 370/392. Corroborated in this search of works with stress in the title by the standard grammar, Bedir Khan & Lescot 1970 §77-78 pp.49-50 (copies we hold lines 2935-2960): 'Dans les mots pris à l'état absolu, il porte généralement sur la dernière syllabe; dans certains cas, cependant, c'est sur l'avant-dernière qu'il tombe. Toute voyelle est susceptible de recevoir l'accent, qu'elle soit longue ou brève.' [In words taken in the absolute state it generally falls on the last syllable; in some cases, however, it falls on the penult. Any vowel can receive the accent, long or short.] — final default with a lexically/morphologically limited penult class (§80-81: 3+-syllable words in -ik and concrete -î), which refines but does not overturn 'fixed-strict' final.

new_statements.quote: p.6 §4: "Le kurde est une langue coulante ; en conséquence ses syllabes ne sont pas nettes et bien articulées. Tout le mot est prononcé comme d'une seule fois, et sort comme d'un seul jet. On appuye presque toujours sur la syllabe finale. En général le mot kurde compte peu de syllabes." — p.45 §43: "On le voit, l'infinitif présent se confond avec les personnes du pluriel du passé indéfini. Ce qui les distingue, c'est le ton ou l'articulation ; car pour l'infinitif, on appuie, on rejette le ton ou la voix sur la dernière syllabe, qui s'accentue pour ainsi dire davantage ; tandis que pour les personnes du pluriel du passé indéfini, on appuie sur les syllabes précédentes."
new_statements.translation: p.6 §4: "Kurdish is a flowing language; consequently its syllables are not crisp and well articulated. The whole word is pronounced as if in one go, and comes out as in a single burst. One almost always stresses the final syllable. In general the Kurdish word has few syllables." — p.45 §43: "As can be seen, the present infinitive coincides with the plural persons of the past indefinite. What distinguishes them is the tone or the articulation; for the infinitive one presses, one throws the tone or the voice onto the last syllable, which is so to speak accented more; whereas for the plural persons of the past indefinite one presses on the preceding syllables."

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final stress, rule 01/001/0001..) and as Hasan 2016 p.370/379 and Bedir Khan & Lescot 1970 §77. The p.45 remark that plural past-indefinite verb forms are stressed on a preceding syllable while the infinitive is final-stressed is a small refinement consistent with Hasan 2016's treatment of stressed stems/non-final stress in certain verb forms and with Bedir Khan & Lescot's 'dans certains cas.. sur l'avant-dernière'. The catalog's 'irrespective of weight' claim is neither confirmed nor denied here (weight is not discussed). Dialect described: Zakho-Gésirah (Zakho–Cizre), i.e. Kurmanji/Bahdini, which is the catalog's variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable 'almost always' (no weight condition mentioned; the book has no dedicated accent section and gives no explicit exception list). A second passage shows stress is used to keep apart homographous verb forms: infinitive kerene 'to do' is stressed on the last syllable, whereas the plural past-indefinite forms (houne kerene 'you did', wane kerene 'they did') are stressed on a preceding (non-final) syllable, i.e. the tense-ending is unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'presque toujours' (almost always) on p.6, and the p.45 case of plural past-indefinite verb forms (e.g. houne kerene, wane kerene) stressed on a non-final syllable, contrasting with the finally-stressed infinitive kerene. No adverb/conjunction or -ik/-î penult class is mentioned.
new_statements.identity_note: Beidar 1926 explicitly describes 'l'idiome.. de Zakho-Gésirah' (preface, PDF page 5: 'Nous avons adopté l'idiome le plus rationnel et le plus répandu : celui de Zakho-Gésirah'), i.e. the Zakho–Cizre (Bahdini/Botani) variety of Northern Kurdish, the same variety as Hasan 2016 (Bahdini) and Bedir Khan & Lescot 1970 (Kurmanji). The author was a Chaldean priest writing from Mosul (preface dated Mosul, 6 February 1925).

sources.quote: L'accent principal dans le mot n'a pas de position fixe. Les quelques règles qui suivent sont données à titre indicatif et comportent de nombreuses exceptions. [...] 1) les formes non verbales. En règle générale l'accent est sur la dernière syllabe. derman, drogue; gerden, cou; wekjî, comme; hemî, tous. [...] En conclusion, l'accent se porte généralement sur la dernière syllabe en ce qui concerne les formes non-verbales. Dans le syntagme verbal, l'accent remonte vers le début du mot et enfin dans l'apostrophe, il est à l'initial.
sources.locator: § 58 L'accent de mot, printed pp. 33-35; conclusion at end of p. 35
sources.note: Default final stress on non-verbal forms (incl. compounds) matches the catalog's fixed: final syllable rule (final stress). The work adds that the main accent 'has no fixed position' and lists morphological exceptions: enclitics (ezafe, indefinite -ek, postpositions, numeral construct) do not move the accent; the diminutive -ûk'/-ik' followed by ezafe draws accent onto the ezafe; the Turkish-origin agentive -çî is stressed; verbs: infinitives of 3+ syllables take penultimate stress (nivist'in, xemilandin), subjunctive stresses the modal prefix bi-, imperative the verbal ending, other verb for…

sources.quote: The experimental words are designed in which the vowels are found at the beginning of the word and in the medial position between a prefix and vowel-initial root in two conditions when the first syllable is either stressed or unstressed. [Table 1: stressed = monosyllables îş, em, av, ol, êş; unstressed = disyllables înan /iːnaːn/, enjam /andʒaːm/, avdan /aːvdaːn/, omêd /omed/, êşan /eʃaːn/] ... As for stress, the results show that it does not affect GS marking in BK. As Table 9 shows that the number of occurrences of the GS is higher in unstressed condition than in the stressed one. The table illustrates that in Kurdish, the vowel-initial unstressed syllables are more marked with glottal stop than the stressed ones. A statistical t test is performed to identify whether the difference is significant. This difference is considered to be not statistically significant (p value is more than 0.05).
sources.locator: p. 11 (section 3.1, Table 1); p. 16 (section 4.5, Table 9: stressed 75/100, unstressed 80/100, p =.3997); p. 17 (section 5)
sources.note: marginal: Acoustic study of the glottal stop in Bahdini Kurdish that tests stress as a conditioning parameter and finds no stress effect; stress is a variable, not the object.

sources.citation: Mohammad, Mazheen Hashim & Hasan, Aveen Mohammed. 2023. Influence of first language on English word stress assignment by Bahdini Kurdish learners of English. Humanities Journal of University of Zakho 11(4): 854-870. doi:10.26436/hjuoz.2023.11.4.1242
sources.quote: Kurdish stress system is said to be uncomplicated. Generally, the final syllable is stressed in words, without any effect of vowel quality, for instance: ziman /zi'mɑːn/ (language), fermanber /faɾm'baɾ/ (employee) and gazinde /gɑːzin'da/ (complaint) are all stressed finally (Shokri, 2002; Abdullah & Ali, 2019). [...] According to Mosa (2009) and Ahmed (1986), some suffixes do not take stress so the penultimate syllable is stressed in the word rather than the final. [...] Two levels of stress are recognized in BK, primary and secondary.
sources.locator: pp. 856-857 (section 2.1.2 Kurdish Stress); language identified p. 855: 'Bahdini Kurdish, a subdialect of North Kurmanji, which is spoken in Iraq'
sources.note: L2 transfer study that characterises Bahdini Kurdish word stress as final-syllable placement and tests its transfer to English stress by 30 learners.

sources.citation: Hasan, Aveen Mohammed. 2017. Northern Kurdish as a stress-accent language. Humanities Journal of University of Zakho 5(3): 868-872. doi:10.26436/2017.5.3.443 (open access)
sources.quote: Instrumental study (30 Duhok speakers, Praat; F0, duration, intensity of segmentally matched stressed vs unstressed syllables, e.g. 'nebe vs nexoşî, 'bibe vs bilind): 'The results indicate that Northern Kurdish is a stress-accent language in that it employs both tonal and non-tonal correlates, especially duration, cues to word-level prominence.' Confirms word-level stress exists and that negative/imperative prefixes ne-/bi- carry stress; silent on default position beyond assuming the final/prefix pattern.

sources.quote: The given examples (4a-b) demonstrated that these pronouns attach to absolute prepositions and do not have any effect on the stress of these word, i.e. the stress remains in its own place. Therefore, if dependent pronouns form a phonological word with their host based on Selkirk's structure (a), the lexical stress must fall on the last syllable. The data of Kurdish language, nonetheless, are contrary to this claim. [p. 53] ... Elements such as pronominal clitics, copula, indefinite marker, coordinating conjunctions or coordinative and genitive are categorized as enclitic. These words are stressless and always attached to the right side of their host. [p. 43] ... As a result, fusional verb inflections form a phonological word with their host and the word stress of the phonological word falls on them. [p. 49]
sources.note: Prosodic-phonology analysis of clitic prepositions and pronouns in Leilakhi Kurdish, using the stress assignment pattern as the diagnostic for clitic-group formation.

sources.note: Not read. Bahdinani is the Duhok-area (Southern Kurmanji) variety of Northern Kurdish, the same variety Hasan 2016/2017 describe. Hasan 2016 (p.370) cites Shokri 2002 as one of the sources for the rule that stress falls on the word-final syllable regardless of length or weight, so the article is expected to confirm the catalog's fixed: final syllable coding; whether it discusses the non-final classes (penult in -ik/-î words per Bedir Khan & Lescot §80-81, heavy-penult adverbs per Hasan 2016) is unknown.
